summary: Specifies the messages of the Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6, used to report errors and carry diagnostic information. Tools such as ping depend on it. It was a draft standard, replaced by RFC 4443.

plainLanguage.summary: If a letter cannot be delivered, the post office sends a note saying why. ICMPv6 is how internet routers send such notes for the newer addresses.

what are the icmpv6 message types

subtitle: The error reports and ping messages that every IPv6 node must understand.

tldr.problem: IPv6 nodes need a way to report packet delivery errors and to run basic diagnostics such as ping, like ICMP does for IPv4.
tldr.mechanism: ICMPv6 uses Next Header value 58 and a common Type, Code and Checksum header. Four error messages (types 1 to 4) and two echo messages (types 128 and 129) are defined, with rules that stop error storms.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2463 was obsoleted by RFC 4443. It had itself replaced RFC 1885.

today: RFC 2463 was a Draft Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 4443, which now defines ICMPv6. It had itself obsoleted RFC 1885.

sections.title: What ICMPv6 Does
sections.content:
ICMPv6 is the Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6. It is based on ICMP for IPv4 (RFC 792) with a number of changes, and it is identified by an IPv6 Next Header value of 58. IPv6 nodes use it to report errors found while processing packets and to perform other internet-layer functions such as diagnostics (ICMPv6 ping).

It is an integral part of IPv6 and MUST be fully implemented by every IPv6 node. This document defines only message formats. Procedures that use the messages, such as Path MTU discovery, are described in other documents, and other documents may add message types subject to the general rules here.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IPv6 computer has to know how to send and understand these little notes about problems, so the network can tell you when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Message Format, Source Address and Checksum
sections.content:
Every message starts with a Type, a Code and a 16-bit Checksum, followed by a message body. A zero in the high-order bit of the Type marks an error message (types 0 to 127). Informational messages use types 128 to 255.

The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the entire ICMPv6 message, prepended with a pseudo-header of IPv6 header fields, using Next Header value 58. Including the pseudo-header is a change from IPv4. The checksum field is set to zero while computing.

The source address of a reply depends on the case. A reply to a message sent to one of the node's unicast addresses must use that same address. A reply to a multicast or anycast message must use a unicast address of the interface that received it. Otherwise the node picks the address most helpful for diagnosis, or the one on the interface that will transmit the message.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a kind, a sub-kind and a check number, so the receiver can tell if the note got scrambled on the way.

sections.title: The Four Error Messages
sections.content:
Destination Unreachable (type 1) is sent when a packet cannot be delivered for reasons other than congestion. Codes are 0 (no route), 1 (administratively prohibited, for example a firewall), 3 (address unreachable) and 4 (port unreachable). Code 2 is not assigned.

Packet Too Big (type 2) MUST be sent by a router that cannot forward a packet because it is larger than the outgoing link's MTU. It carries that MTU and feeds Path MTU Discovery.

Time Exceeded (type 3) has code 0 for hop limit exceeded in transit and code 1 for fragment reassembly time exceeded. A router that decrements a Hop Limit to zero MUST discard the packet and send code 0.

Parameter Problem (type 4) uses code 0 for an erroneous header field, 1 for an unrecognized Next Header and 2 for an unrecognized IPv6 option. A Pointer gives the octet offset of the problem in the invoking packet.

Each error message includes as much of the offending packet as fits without exceeding the minimum IPv6 MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of bad news: I cannot find that place, your parcel is too big, it took too long to arrive, and something on the label does not make sense.

sections.title: Echo and Error Rules
sections.content:
An Echo Request (type 128) carries an Identifier, a Sequence Number and optional data. Every node MUST implement an echo responder that answers with an Echo Reply (type 129) returning the identifier, sequence number and data entirely and unmodified. A node SHOULD also provide an application interface for sending requests, for diagnostic use.

To keep error traffic under control, an ICMPv6 error message MUST NOT be sent in response to another ICMPv6 error, to a packet sent to a multicast address (with two exceptions: Packet Too Big, and Parameter Problem code 2 for certain options), to a link-layer multicast or broadcast packet, or to a packet whose source address does not identify a single node, such as the unspecified address. A node MUST also rate-limit the error messages it sends, with configurable limits and a conservative default, for example at most once per second.

Unknown error messages MUST be passed to the upper layer, while unknown informational messages MUST be silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Ping is like calling out and waiting for an echo. And nobody is allowed to answer a bad-news note with another bad-news note, or everyone would end up sending notes forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ICMP exchanges can be authenticated with the IP Authentication Header. A node SHOULD include one when a security association exists for the destination. Received messages with an incorrect Authentication Header MUST be ignored and discarded. Administrators SHOULD be able to configure a node to ignore unauthenticated ICMP messages, with a default that allows them.

The RFC lists attacks: spoofing the source, redirecting the reply, altering message fields, and denial of service by sending back-to-back erroneous packets. Authentication or encryption addresses the first three, and error rate limiting addresses the last.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature on the note shows who really sent it, and a limit on how many notes you send stops anyone from flooding the mailbox.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type; 0 to 127 are errors, 128 to 255 informational.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Additional granularity depending on the type.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Detects corruption of the message and parts of the IPv6 header.

items.label: Packet Too Big
items.desc: Packet exceeds the next link's MTU.

items.label: Time Exceeded
items.desc: Hop limit or reassembly time ran out.

items.label: Parameter Problem
items.desc: A header field or option could not be processed.
